Hijacked Hotel Wi-Fi Pushes Fake Updates to Deliver Surveillance Malware

The Hacker News
2026-08-01 15 use cases 10 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A fake browser update served over hijacked hotel Wi-Fi has been used to deliver CornFlake, a remote access trojan (RAT) that can capture webcam images, microphone audio, and keystrokes, Microsoft said in its latest report. Researchers track the operation as CaptiveCrunch and attribute it to Storm-2945. It assesses Storm-2945 to be an operational sub-cluster of Midnight Blizzard, also known as

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ClickFix fake-update command referencing CaptiveCrunch infrastructure · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Hijacked Hotel Wi-Fi Pushes Fake Updates to Deliver Surveillance Malware
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] CornFlake RAT self-copy to %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe · [LLM] CornFlake service registration 'svchost32' / 'Cloud Sync Service' · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Microsoft device code authentication flow phishing sign-in · [LLM] CaptiveCrunch C2 / phishing infrastructure network callback · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] ChocoShell token theft from TokenBroker .tbres cache · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
CornFlake RAT self-copy to %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe AIInstallation High
Hunts the CornFlake Go implant staging itself as %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe — a masquerade of the legitimate System32 svchost.exe that never legitimately lives in Roaming AppData. This is the on-disk footprint of the CaptiveCrunch implant before service registration. Rationale: Anchors on the exact implant path %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe named in Microsoft's report; the '32'-suffixed svchost in Roaming AppData is not a real Windows binary, giving near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://securityaffairs.com/196441/apt/russian-hackers-hijack-hotel-wi-fi-to-steal-microsoft-365-tokens.html
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A niche third-party 'svchost32' utility legitimately installed under Roaming (extremely rare)
  • Security researcher / malware analyst detonating a CornFlake sample in a monitored VM
  • Backup or EDR sync agent that copies quarantined samples into a Roaming staging folder
  • Custom LOB app that unfortunately named its binary svchost32.exe (validate publisher/signer)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msmpeng.exe","sense.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "Windows Defender")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull SHA256 of the created file and the InitiatingProcess; check signer status and whether the parent is a browser/terminal from a captive-portal 'update'. 2) Contain: isolate the host in Defender, kill the svchost32 process tree, and quarantine %APPDATA%\svchost32\. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC 'CornFlake service Cloud Sync Service' and UC 'ChocoShell Token Broker theft' on the same DeviceId; check outbound to the CaptiveCrunch C2 IOCs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName =~ "svchost32.exe"
| where FolderPath has @"\AppData\Roaming\svchost32\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName =~ "svchost32.exe"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\AppData\Roaming\svchost32\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CornFlake service registration 'svchost32' / 'Cloud Sync Service' AIInstallation High
Detects registration of the CornFlake persistence service — Windows service name svchost32 with display name 'Cloud Sync Service' and description 'Synchronizes files with the cloud storage provider'. This is the service-based persistence layer of the CaptiveCrunch implant, restored by a watchdog if removed. Rationale: Uses the literal service name (svchost32), display name ('Cloud Sync Service'), and ImagePath (svchost32.exe) from Microsoft's write-up — all three are unique campaign strings, so any one match is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://www.secnews.gr/en/725008/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-xenodocheia-wifi/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1036.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Services
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate cloud-sync product coincidentally using display name 'Cloud Sync Service' (verify ImagePath is NOT svchost32.exe in Roaming)
  • EDR/backup agent re-registering a sync service after update
  • Golden-image build process installing sync services (validate against approved software list)
  • Analyst detonation of the sample in a sandbox VM
Suppression filter
| where not (ServiceFileName has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\") and ServiceFileName !has "svchost32.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm ServiceFileName resolves to %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe (not a signed vendor path); note SubjectUserName that created it. 2) Contain: stop and delete the svchost32 service (sc delete), isolate host — note the watchdog will attempt restore, so remove the file drop, Run key, and scheduled task together. 3) Hunt: enumerate scheduled tasks and HKCU\...\Run entries pointing to svchost32.exe; check other travelers who used the same hotel network for the same service.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Services\svchost32"
    or (RegistryValueName =~ "DisplayName" and RegistryValueData has "Cloud Sync Service")
    or (RegistryValueName =~ "ImagePath" and RegistryValueData has "svchost32.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4697
| where ServiceName =~ "svchost32" or ServiceFileName has "svchost32.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceStartType, ServiceAccount, SubjectUserName, SubjectDomainName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ChocoShell token theft from TokenBroker .tbres cache AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the ChocoShell in-memory PowerShell stealer reading Microsoft 365 / Entra ID access, refresh and WAM tokens from .tbres files in the Token Broker cache. Any script interpreter (or the svchost32 implant) touching %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\TokenBroker\Cache\*.tbres is anomalous — legitimate access is by the WAM/TokenBroker host only. Rationale: Anchors on the exact artifact ChocoShell steals — .tbres files in \Microsoft\TokenBroker\Cache\ — scoped to script interpreters and the svchost32 implant; the public TBRESDecryptor tool confirms this is the real WAM/M365 token store, and normal readers are only the TokenBroker host. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://github.com/shackcrack007/TBRESDecryptor
ATT&CKT1528 T1539 T1555
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A red-team/purple-team exercise running TBRESDecryptor or ROADtools
  • IT PowerShell script auditing token cache health (rare, validate signer/repo)
  • Endpoint DLP agent indexing AppData (should be its own signed process, not powershell.exe)
  • Developer debugging WAM SSO with a PowerShell helper
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Windows\System32\", @"\Windows\SysWOW64\") and InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "backgroundTaskHost.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full PowerShell command line / script block (correlate with AMSI ScriptControlScanInfo) and the acting user's UPN. 2) Contain: from Entra ID, revoke that user's refresh tokens (revokeSignInSessions) and force password + MFA re-registration; the .tbres theft yields replayable tokens without a browser. 3) Hunt: review SigninLogs/AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs for token replay from new IPs/ASNs for that user; pivot to UC 'Device code authentication flow' and the C2 IOC UC.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"\Microsoft\TokenBroker\Cache\"
| where FileName endswith ".tbres"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","svchost32.exe")
    or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\AppData\Roaming\svchost32\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Microsoft\TokenBroker\Cache\"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".tbres"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","svchost32.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Microsoft device code authentication flow phishing sign-in AICommand & Control Medium
Detects successful Entra ID sign-ins that used the OAuth device code flow — the vector CaptiveCrunch landing pages have abused since 16 July to obtain MFA-satisfied, attacker-controlled sessions. Device code flow is rare in most tenants and is Microsoft's recommended Conditional-Access block, so any success is worth review. Rationale: Article states CaptiveCrunch landing pages redirect guests into Microsoft's device code flow since 16 July; device code sign-ins are the article-specific pivot and Microsoft explicitly recommends blocking them via Conditional Access, so the flow's use is inherently high-signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://securityaffairs.com/196441/apt/russian-hackers-hijack-hotel-wi-fi-to-steal-microsoft-365-tokens.html
ATT&CKT1528 T1566.002
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate device-code onboarding of IoT/CLI tools (Azure CLI 'az login --use-device-code', PowerShell Connect-AzAccount)
  • Conference-room / kiosk device provisioning
  • Developers authenticating headless apps or WSL sessions
  • Smart-TV or streaming-device Microsoft account linking
Suppression filter
| where not (AppDisplayName has_any ("Microsoft Azure CLI","Microsoft Azure PowerShell") and ConditionalAccessStatus == "success")
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the IPAddress/Location and UserAgent of the device-code sign-in against the user's normal pattern and whether they were traveling; correlate the sign-in IP with the CaptiveCrunch C2 ranges. 2) Contain: revoke sessions/refresh tokens for the account and, org-wide, deploy a Conditional Access policy blocking device code flow where not required. 3) Hunt: review subsequent app consents, mailbox rules, and token replay from the same session; check other users sharing the venue/IP.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code"
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Application, ApplicationId, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, Country, City, DeviceName, UserAgent, ClientAppUsed
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where tostring(AuthenticationProcessingDetails) has "Device Code"
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, Location, UserAgent, ClientAppUsed, ConditionalAccessStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CaptiveCrunch C2 / phishing infrastructure network callback AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host resolving or connecting to the confirmed CaptiveCrunch Microsoft-impersonating domains (m365-owa.com, owa-ms365.com, ms365-device.com, ms365-live.com, deltaode.com) or the four campaign C2 IPs. Covers both the fake-update/token-phishing landing pages and CornFlake implant callbacks. Rationale: Direct IOC match on the five Microsoft-impersonating domains ReliaQuest and Microsoft both documented plus the four extracted C2 IPs; exact-value matches on known-bad infrastructure are inherently high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://securityaffairs.com/196441/apt/russian-hackers-hijack-hotel-wi-fi-to-steal-microsoft-365-tokens.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment/sandbox appliance in the org detonating the IOCs
  • Security researcher browsing the phishing domains for analysis from a sanctioned host
  • A parked/sinkholed domain reused by a benign service after takedown (validate IP still hostile)
  • DNS logging test traffic from a SOC validation run
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("SANDBOX","MALWARE-ANALYSIS","TI-DETONATE"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess making the connection — a browser suggests landing-page interaction; svchost32.exe/powershell suggests active implant C2. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block all five domains and four IPs at proxy/firewall/DNS, and add them to the TI platform. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for any historical resolution of these IOCs and pivot to the CornFlake implant-drop and Token Broker theft UCs on matching hosts.

ClickFix fake-update command referencing CaptiveCrunch infrastructure AIDelivery High
Detects the CaptiveCrunch ClickFix delivery step: a victim pastes an attacker-supplied command into a terminal/Run dialog and a script interpreter (PowerShell, cmd, mshta, curl, certutil, bitsadmin) executes with a command line that references the campaign's phishing/C2 domains or IPs. Captures the actual download cradle that pulls the fake browser/OS update. Rationale: Combines the ClickFix TTP (interpreter running a pasted command) with the campaign's specific infrastructure strings in the command line, surfacing the actual fake-update download cradle rather than a generic interpreter launch. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/hijacked-hotel-wifi-pushes-fake.html • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC/analyst running a validation command that includes an IOC domain for testing
  • Threat-hunter pasting an IOC into a terminal while investigating
  • Sanctioned network diagnostics that curl a lookalike domain during takedown validation
  • Automated IOC sweep script that references the domains/IPs as arguments
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("IOC-sweep","threat-hunt","validate-detection"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full ProcessCommandLine to see what was downloaded/executed and identify the parent (explorer.exe = Run-dialog paste is classic ClickFix); note the user and host location. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the interpreter and any spawned installer, block the referenced IOCs. 3) Hunt: check for the CornFlake drop (%APPDATA%\svchost32\), the svchost32 service, scheduled tasks/Run keys, and Token Broker .tbres access on the same host; brief the user on captive-portal update lures.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("m365-owa.com","owa-ms365.com","ms365-device.com","ms365-live.com","deltaode.com","31.57.243.154","104.194.159.150","38.146.28.75","89.124.79.98")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("m365-owa.com","owa-ms365.com","ms365-device.com","ms365-live.com","deltaode.com","31.57.243.154","104.194.159.150","38.146.28.75","89.124.79.98")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1555.003

logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")

    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ApostropheCMS auth-bypass symptom: protected piece-type endpoint 401/403 → 200 transition AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the impact of CVE-2026-53609: a source IP that previously received 401/403 on /api/v1/@apostrophecms/user or /global begins receiving 200 responses, without any preceding successful login. This is the process-wide publicApiCheck() bypass observed on the wire. Rationale: Targets the advisory's confirmed observable: /api/v1/@apostrophecms/user and /global flipping from notfound(401/403) to a valid 200 paginated response for unauthenticated callers. Login-IP exclusion asserts the 'unauthenticated' precondition the article emphasises. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6h5j-32cf-4253 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/apostrophe/CVE-2026-53609/

  • publicApiProjection intentionally configured on a piece-type, so unauthenticated 200s are by-design for that endpoint
  • Load balancer / uptime monitor hitting the endpoint from an IP that also fails auth elsewhere
  • CDN edge caching a 200 response and serving it to varied client IPs

ApostropheCMS exploit chain: unauth PATCH to /@apostrophecms/global → 200 GET on /user within 30s AIExploitation High
Correlates the two-step CVE-2026-53609 exploit: a PATCH to /api/v1/@apostrophecms/* from an IP that never authenticated, immediately followed (≤30s) by a successful 200 GET on a normally-protected piece-type endpoint from the same IP. Sequencing raises confidence over either event alone. Rationale: Encodes the PoC step sequence from the advisory (Step 3 PATCH poisoning -> Step 4 unauthenticated 200 on /user) as a same-source temporal join with a 30s window and a never-authenticated precondition, yielding a high-fidelity, low-FP correlation. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6h5j-32cf-4253 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/apostrophe/CVE-2026-53609/
ATT&CKT1190 T1548
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Automated vulnerability scanner running the exact PoC sequence during an authorized assessment
  • Editor whose auth cookie is stripped from access logs, so a legitimate PATCH+GET pair looks unauthenticated
  • Reverse proxy that rewrites method/path causing spurious PATCH-then-GET pairing
  • publicApiProjection legitimately enabled, making the trailing GET a by-design 200
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Retrieve both correlated requests for the CIp; confirm the PATCH body carried $pullAll/__proto__ and the GET returned a real result set rather than notfound. 2) CONTAIN: Restart the Node.js process to purge the polluted prototype, block the source IP, and rotate/disable any editor account whose token appears on the PATCH. 3) HUNT: Expand the window to enumerate every unauthenticated 200 to all piece-type endpoints after PatchTime; check for data exfiltration volume and pivot on the editor account for prior suspicious PATCH activity.
let win = 30s;
let lookback = 2d;
let loggedInIPs = AppServiceHTTPLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
    | where CsUriStem has "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/login/login" and ScStatus == 200
    | distinct CIp;
let patches = AppServiceHTTPLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
    | where CsMethod =~ "PATCH" and CsUriStem startswith "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/"
    | where CIp !in (loggedInIPs)
    | project PatchTime = TimeGenerated, CIp, PatchUri = CsUriStem;
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where CsMethod =~ "GET" and ScStatus == 200
| where CsUriStem in~ ("/api/v1/@apostrophecms/user","/api/v1/@apostrophecms/global")
| where CIp !in (loggedInIPs)
| join kind=inner patches on CIp
| where TimeGenerated between (PatchTime .. PatchTime + win)
| project PatchTime, GetTime = TimeGenerated, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, PatchTime), CIp, PatchUri, GetUri = CsUriStem
| order by PatchTime desc

Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: For each host/site returned, confirm it is genuinely ApostropheCMS and determine the running version (check package.json / release notes / vendor). 2) CONTAIN: For any instance <=4.30.0, prioritise upgrade to 4.31.0 and apply the __proto__/constructor/prototype path-segment rejection; restrict editor account provisioning. 3) HUNT: On confirmed-vulnerable hosts, run the payload-detection and auth-bypass UCs retroactively over 30d to check for prior exploitation.

            by CsHost
| order by Requests desc

CornFlake RAT persistence via svchost32.exe masquerade in %APPDATA% AIInstallation High
Hunts Storm-2945's CornFlake implant, which copies itself to %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe and registers as a Windows service 'svchost32' (display name 'Cloud Sync Service') to masquerade as the legitimate System32 svchost.exe. Legitimate svchost.exe only ever runs from %SystemRoot%\System32, so any svchost32.exe under a user profile path is malicious by construction. Rationale: Anchored on the exact drop path %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe and service name 'svchost32'/'Cloud Sync Service' from the article; corroborated by ReliaQuest and The Hacker News. A binary named svchost32.exe outside System32 has no legitimate use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/hijacked-hotel-wi-fi-pushes-fake.html • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1036.005 T1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A niche third-party app that legitimately ships a file literally named svchost32.exe in AppData (extremely rare; none known)
  • Security researcher / IR analyst detonating the CornFlake sample in a sandbox on a monitored host
  • EDR sample-detonation or red-team emulation of this exact campaign
  • Backup/restore of an already-infected profile re-writing the path
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the SHA256 of svchost32.exe and confirm the parent process and the '\svchost32\svchost32.exe' path is under a user profile (never System32). Check for a service named svchost32 with display 'Cloud Sync Service'. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, stop and delete the svchost32 service, remove the Run key and scheduled task pointing at the binary, and force-revoke the user's Entra sessions/tokens (traveler likely token-compromised). 3) HUNT: Sweep for the same path/service org-wide, and pivot to DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound connections from svchost32.exe and to the doppelganger M365 domains/IOC IPs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath endswith @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe" or FileName =~ "svchost32.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AccountName, ReportId
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(SecurityEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where EventID == 4688 | where NewProcessName endswith @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe" | where SubjectUserName !endswith "$" | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Evidence=NewProcessName, Detail=CommandLine, Actor=SubjectUserName),
(SecurityEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where EventID == 4697 | where ServiceName =~ "svchost32" or ServiceFileName endswith @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe" | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Evidence=ServiceName, Detail=ServiceFileName, Actor=SubjectUserName)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Endpoint connections to Storm-2945 CaptiveCrunch AiTM doppelganger infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts network connections and DNS lookups to the Storm-2945 doppelganger domains that mimic Microsoft 365 services (ms365-device.com, ms365-live.com, m365-owa.com, owa-ms365.com) and the campaign's actor-controlled IP infrastructure used for adversary-in-the-middle device-code phishing and M365 token theft. These are hard IOCs — any hit indicates a traveler routed through the CaptiveCrunch AiTM proxy. Rationale: Uses the article's exact doppelganger domain list and pre-extracted actor IP set (Block 2), cross-checked against ReliaQuest's write-up of the same infrastructure. These are unique lookalike domains with zero legitimate business use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/ • https://securityaffairs.com/196441/apt/russian-hackers-hijack-hotel-wi-fi-to-steal-microsoft-365-tokens.html
ATT&CKT1557 T1539 T1566.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security tool / TI feed pre-fetching or sinkholing these IOC domains for analysis
  • Analyst manually browsing to the domain during investigation from a corporate host
  • Passive DNS / URL-scanning services running from the monitored range
  • IP reuse after takedown where the IP is reassigned to a benign host (verify domain hit alongside IP)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify which user/device connected and whether the connection carried an M365 auth flow (browser process, Referer to login.microsoftonline.com). Confirm the device was on untrusted Wi-Fi (hotel/conference). 2) CONTAIN: Revoke the user's Entra refresh tokens and sign-in sessions immediately, require re-registration of MFA, and block the domains/IPs at proxy and firewall. 3) HUNT: Check Entra sign-in logs for the same user authenticating from the actor IPs and for any new device registration; sweep the endpoint for CornFlake (svchost32.exe) delivered on the same session.

| where RemoteUrl has_any(target_domains) or RemoteIP in (target_ips)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ReportId

(DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Name has_any (target_domains) | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, Result)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Entra ID sign-in or session from Storm-2945 AiTM device-code phishing infrastructure AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects successful Entra ID authentications originating from Storm-2945's actor-controlled IP infrastructure, the tail end of the CaptiveCrunch device-code AiTM flow where a phished traveler's device code authenticates the attacker's session. Anchors on the campaign's confirmed IP set as the sign-in source. Rationale: Anchors on the article's actor IP set as the authentication source — a successful M365 sign-in from CaptiveCrunch infrastructure is a direct token-theft indicator; Volexity independently documents the same device-code AiTM technique for this actor. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2025/02/13/multiple-russian-threat-actors-targeting-microsoft-device-code-authentication/ • https://phishingtackle.com/blog/russian-hackers-use-microsoft-device-code-phishing-in-targeted-attacks
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1528 T1098.005
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An IOC IP later reassigned by its hosting provider to a benign VPN/proxy a legitimate user transits
  • Threat-intel enrichment appliance replaying sign-in test traffic
  • Corporate egress NAT coincidentally sharing a subnet with a taken-down IOC (verify exact /32)
  • Analyst reproducing the auth flow from an actor IP in a lab tenant
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the sign-in succeeded (ErrorCode/ResultType 0) and identify the app (Graph, OWA) and whether a new device was registered in the same window. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke all refresh tokens for the account, disable the account or force password reset + MFA re-enrollment, and remove any attacker-registered device from Entra. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the account to Graph/EWS mail-access and any OAuth app consent grants; check the user's endpoint for CornFlake and correlate to the doppelganger-domain connections from UC2.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where IPAddress in (target_ips)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Application, ApplicationId, IPAddress, Country, City, ClientAppUsed, DeviceTrustType, ConditionalAccessStatus, ReportId
| order by Timestamp desc

union isfuzzy=true
(SigninLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where IPAddress in (target_ips) | where ResultType == 0 | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, IPAddress, Location, ClientAppUsed, RiskLevelDuringSignIn),
(AuditLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where OperationName has "device" and Category =~ "Device" | extend Actor=tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), ActorIp=tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress) | where ActorIp in (target_ips) | project TimeGenerated, OperationName, Actor, ActorIp, Result)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ClickFix execution reaching CaptiveCrunch infrastructure or dropping svchost32 AIDelivery High
Detects the CaptiveCrunch ClickFix chain where a user is socially engineered (fake browser/OS update) into running a script interpreter whose command line reaches Storm-2945's doppelganger domains/IOC IPs or references the CornFlake drop path svchost32. Anchors the generic ClickFix pattern to this campaign's concrete IOCs to avoid template noise. Rationale: Pairs the ClickFix execution primitive (interpreter launch) with the campaign's hard IOCs (doppelganger domains, actor IPs, svchost32 drop path) so it fires only on this campaign, not on generic scripting — combination is high-fidelity per the article's ClickFix delivery description. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/hijacked-hotel-wi-fi-pushes-fake.html

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Threat-hunting query copy-pasted into a console leaving IOC strings in a shell history/command line
  • Sinkhole or research tooling curling the IOC domains for analysis
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Read the full command line — confirm which IOC it hit (domain download vs svchost32 reference) and the parent process (explorer.exe/browser indicates ClickFix paste). 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the interpreter and any child svchost32.exe, and revoke the user's Entra tokens (traveler credential exposure). 3) HUNT: Pivot to DeviceFileEvents for the svchost32 drop and DeviceNetworkEvents for follow-on C2 to the IOC IPs; sweep other travelers for the same ClickFix command shape.

CornFlake C2 egress from masqueraded svchost32.exe in AppData AICommand & Control High
Detects outbound network connections initiated by the CornFlake implant running as svchost32.exe from a user AppData path. The legitimate svchost.exe lives only in System32 and its network activity is service-mediated, so public-internet egress from a profile-resident svchost32.exe is CornFlake C2 / data exfiltration beaconing. Rationale: Anchors on the CornFlake implant image/path (svchost32.exe under AppData, from the article) making outbound public connections — behaviorally impossible for the real System32 svchost.exe, so any hit is CornFlake beaconing. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573 T1036.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sandbox detonation of the CornFlake sample generating C2 traffic on a monitored host
  • Red-team emulation using a binary named svchost32.exe
  • A misconfigured third-party tool coincidentally named svchost32.exe (none known)
  • EDR telemetry replay/testing environments
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm InitiatingProcessFolderPath is a user AppData path and capture the RemoteIP/RemoteUrl destinations (correlate to the campaign IOC IPs). 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, terminate svchost32.exe, remove its service/Run key/scheduled task persistence, and block the C2 destinations. 3) HUNT: Retrieve collected-data artifacts (keylogger/screenshot/audio files), revoke the traveler's Entra tokens, and sweep the fleet for the same process-to-public-IP pattern and the svchost32 drop path.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost32.exe" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ReportId
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost32.exe" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ReportId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")

NocoBase CVE-2026-52887 SQLi in /api/myInAppChannels:list filter[latestMsgReceiveTimestamp][$lt] AIExploitation High
Hunts the exact injection vector: a request to the myInAppChannels:list resource whose filter carries the latestMsgReceiveTimestamp[$lt] parameter loaded with PostgreSQL SQLi primitives (PG_SLEEP, stacked COPY ... TO PROGRAM, CASE WHEN oracles). The legit value of $lt is an epoch integer, so any SQL keyword in this parameter is high-fidelity exploitation of CVE-2026-52887. Rationale: Uses the exact vulnerable resource string 'myInAppChannels', the injectable parameter 'latestMsgReceiveTimestamp', and the article's live-verified payload tokens PG_SLEEP / COPY ... TO PROGRAM / CASE WHEN. A legit $lt is an integer epoch, so any SQL keyword in this param is exploitation, not noise. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@nocobase/plugin-notification-in-app-message/CVE-2026-52887/ • https://github.com/nocobase/nocobase/pull/9001
ATT&CKT1190

  • Vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Nuclei) firing the CVE-2026-52887 template
  • Security researcher validating the patch on a staging host
  • WAF in monitor-only mode logging blocked-but-recorded attempts
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("10.0.0.0")  // add authorized scanner / pentest source IPs here
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request URL and source IP; confirm the $lt value contains SQL rather than a bare integer, and check the response status/latency (a ~5s delay = successful PG_SLEEP oracle). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/proxy, and if the request succeeded, treat the NocoBase DB container as compromised — rotate the super-admin credential and disable allowSignUp. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP for prior /api/auth:signUp and /api/auth:signIn calls, and check the Postgres host for postgres-spawned shell processes (UC3).

NocoBase anonymous signup then immediate myInAppChannels access (CVE-2026-52887 pre-exploit) AIDelivery Medium
Correlates a successful anonymous account creation via /api/auth:signUp (enabled by the default allowSignUp:true) with a request to the vulnerable /api/myInAppChannels:list resource from the same source IP within minutes. This is the article's stated exploitation prerequisite: sign up, sign in, then hit the loggedIn-ACL endpoint. Rationale: Chains the two article-named endpoints — /api/auth:signUp (default allowSignUp:true) and the vulnerable /api/myInAppChannels:list — on a shared source IP inside a 10-minute window, matching the documented signup→signin→exploit flow. Same-IP correlation strips ordinary user browsing. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@nocobase/plugin-notification-in-app-message/CVE-2026-52887/

PostgreSQL backend spawning shell/LOLBin (COPY ... TO PROGRAM RCE, CVE-2026-52887) AIExploitation High
Detects the RCE tail of CVE-2026-52887: the PostgreSQL backend process (running as uid=999 postgres in the DB container) spawning a shell or command binary via COPY ... TO PROGRAM. A postgres process should never fork sh/bash/id/curl, so this parent→child pair is a near-certain indicator of stacked-statement SQLi execution. Rationale: Anchored on the article's confirmed RCE mechanics: COPY ... TO PROGRAM runs shell as uid=999(postgres). A postgres parent forking sh/bash/id/curl is behaviourally impossible in normal operation, giving a very low-FP endpoint signal that complements the web-layer UC1. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@nocobase/plugin-notification-in-app-message/CVE-2026-52887/ • https://github.com/nocobase/nocobase/pull/9001
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Postgres archive_command / restore_command configured to call a shell script (WAL archiving)
  • PL/Perl or PL/Python stored procedures legitimately invoking helpers
  • DBA maintenance job using COPY TO PROGRAM for legitimate ETL/export
  • Container init or healthcheck script mis-parented under the postgres process tree
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "archive_command" and ProcessCommandLine !has "pg_wal"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child ProcessCommandLine — article shows payloads like 'id > /tmp/PWN_VERIFY.txt' and COPY reads of the users table; check the DB host /tmp for dropped files. 2) Contain: isolate the DB container, kill the spawned process tree, and rotate the exfiltrable secrets (users.password PBKDF2 hashes, admin id=1). 3) Hunt: correlate back to the originating web request (UC1) via timestamp, review any archive_command config to rule out benign use, and audit the postgres role for the rolsuper attribute that enabled COPY TO PROGRAM.

Hunts endpoint DNS resolutions and network connections to the hard-coded C2 domains and VPS IPs published for the OctLurk/SilkLurk/LurkProxy Central Asia campaign (e.g. dns.multitoconference.com, dns.ssentialserv.xyz connectivity check, 154.196.162.76). These indicators uniquely identify the campaign's command-and-control channel and are shared with the SilentRaid/MystRodX/TrustFall infrastructure. Rationale: Uses the campaign's hard-coded C2 domains (dns.multitoconference.com OctLurk beacon, dns.ssentialserv.xyz LurkProxy connectivity check) and the 11 VPS IPs, three of which Kaspersky/STS confirm overlap with SilentRaid/MystRodX/TrustFall infrastructure — high-fidelity, cross-sourced indicators. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/ • https://gbhackers.com/octlurk-and-silklurk-backdoors/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/01/china-linked-uat-7290-targets-telecoms.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • digital.leroymerlin.com may collide with legitimate Leroy Merlin retail traffic on non-target networks — validate the resolved IP against the VPS list
  • Security appliances/sandboxes detonating samples and generating the same C2 lookups
  • Threat-intel enrichment or DNS sinkhole services pre-resolving IOC domains
  • DNS logging proxies replaying historic queries during migration
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl == "digital.leroymerlin.com" and RemoteIP !in ("154.196.162.76","45.138.157.165","95.179.210.138","45.77.136.228","95.179.141.26","45.32.152.50","212.11.39.138","195.86.120.2","154.196.187.73","45.61.149.112","64.7.198.130"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process (InitiatingProcessFileName/ContextImageFileName) that resolved/connected to the IOC and whether the host is a Central Asian government/ministry asset in scope. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host, block the domain+IP at the firewall/DNS, and capture memory (both families run in-memory with a minimal on-disk loader). 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for the loader on disk, secretsdump/fscan/pp.txt activity, an AnyDesk-named keylogger, and lateral net-use to admin shares; sweep the fleet for any other IOC-list domain or IP.

OctLurk/SilkLurk/LurkProxy/PlugX known sample hash execution or drop AIInstallation Medium
Alerts on process execution, image load, or file write matching the 16 MD5 hashes published for the OctLurk, SilkLurk, LurkProxy and side-loaded PlugX samples. Because both families are victim-specific and memory-resident, catching the minimal on-disk loader by hash is the cleanest execution-stage signal. Rationale: Directly uses the 16 published MD5s spanning OctLurk, SilkLurk, LurkProxy and side-loaded PlugX; hash IOCs are the highest-fidelity execution/install signal for memory-resident, victim-encoded loaders that otherwise leave minimal disk footprint. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/ • https://gbhackers.com/octlurk-and-silklurk-backdoors/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1574.002 T1055
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analysts detonating the samples in a monitored analysis VM
  • AV/EDR quarantine copies retaining the file and re-triggering file events
  • Threat-intel researchers storing IOC samples on a corporate share
  • Hash collision is effectively nil for MD5 at this scale but re-used loader stub across benign packers is theoretically possible
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any (@"\\Sandbox\\", @"\\Analysis\\", @"\\Quarantine\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the hit is on a production endpoint (not an analysis sandbox) and record host, user, path and initiating process. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill/quarantine the sample, and capture volatile memory before reboot since the real payload lives in RAM. 3) Hunt: pull the loader's parent chain, look for the drive-serial/computer-name-keyed decode routine, and sweep for the C2 IOCs, secretsdump, fscan/pp.txt and AnyDesk-named keylogger across the estate.

union
(DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where MD5 in (hashes) | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="ProcessCreate", MD5, FileName, FolderPath, Actor=InitiatingProcessCommandLine),

Impacket secretsdump domain-controller hash extraction AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts command-line invocation of Impacket's secretsdump against domain controllers, matching the campaign's post-compromise step of harvesting password hashes from DCs. Anchors on secretsdump / -just-dc flags rather than LSASS access, so it complements existing credential-theft rules. Rationale: Article states hashes were harvested from domain controllers using Impacket's secretsdump.py; the secretsdump string plus -just-dc* flags are the tool's canonical invocation and rarely legitimate in production. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/new-backdoors-let-hackers-keylog/
ATT&CKT1003.006 T1003.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Red-team / purple-team exercises legitimately running Impacket
  • AD security assessments using secretsdump for auditing
  • A pentest tool named similarly living in a security team's toolkit share
  • Detection engineering validating this very rule with an atomic test
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\\RedTeam\\" and DeviceName !in~ ("PENTEST-01","SECAUDIT-01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the source host/user is an authorized pentest asset; check the target (DC hostname) and whether -just-dc dumped NTDS. 2) Contain: disable the executing account, isolate the host, and treat all domain credentials as potentially compromised — begin krbtgt double-reset planning. 3) Hunt: correlate with the campaign C2 IOCs, look for prior remote-interactive logons to the DC, Pandora RC remote access, and subsequent lateral net-use to admin shares.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("secretsdump", "-just-dc-ntlm", "-just-dc-user", "-just-dc ")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where CommandLine has_any ("secretsdump", "-just-dc-ntlm", "-just-dc-user", "-just-dc ")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AnyDesk-masquerading keylogger execution from non-standard path AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a process named like AnyDesk that is NOT the genuine signed AnyDesk binary, matching the campaign's keylogger that masquerades as AnyDesk to evade detection. Filters out the legitimate AnyDesk Software GmbH signed install. Rationale: Article states the keylogger 'masquerades as AnyDesk to sidestep detection'; matching an anydesk-named binary that lacks the AnyDesk Software GmbH signature and runs from a user-writable path isolates the impostor from genuine remote-support usage. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/new-backdoors-let-hackers-keylog/
ATT&CKT1056.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Portable/unpacked AnyDesk run from Downloads by a legitimate support tech (usually still signed — the Company filter catches it)
  • Software-deployment staging AnyDesk to a ProgramData cache before install
  • Renamed legitimate AnyDesk copies by IT for allow-listing tests
  • Older AnyDesk builds with missing version metadata
Suppression filter
| where isnotempty(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName) and ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !has "AnyDesk"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the binary's signer/hash — a genuine AnyDesk is signed by 'AnyDesk Software GmbH'; an unsigned/mismatched one from a user path is the keylogger. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the file, and force-reset credentials typed on that host (keystrokes are captured). 3) Hunt: look for the parent loader, browser-password decryption of Chrome/Firefox, secretsdump, and outbound C2 to the campaign domains from the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has "anydesk"
| where not (FolderPath has @"\AnyDesk\" and (ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "AnyDesk" or ProcessVersionInfoProductName has "AnyDesk"))
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Users\", @"\AppData\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Public\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "anydesk"
| where not (ActingProcessName has @"\AnyDesk\" and ActingProcessFileCompany has "AnyDesk")
| where ActingProcessName has_any (@"\Users\", @"\AppData\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Public\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessFileCompany, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: AnyDesk-Masquerading Keylogger From Non-Standard Path
id: 6a8b2f14-9c0d-4e73-a1b6-3f2c8d5e7a90
description: Detects a process named anydesk.exe running outside the legitimate signed AnyDesk install path (OctLurk/SilkLurk keylogger masquerade)
references:
