``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| join type=inner user

The Hacker News
2026-07-31 12 use cases 5 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Designed for input-constrained devices like smart TVs, printers, and so on, the device authorization login flow has been adopted by a wide range of apps and use-cases that it wasn't originally

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Phishing email delivering a Microsoft/GitHub device-login URL · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Entra ID device-code grant to first-time user via Microsoft Authentication Broker · [LLM] Device-code sign-in from country never seen for the user (stolen-code redemption) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] New Entra device registration shortly after a device-code grant (PRT persistence)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Stolen device-code token fanning out to multiple SSO resources within the hour · [LLM] Bulk mailbox and SharePoint collection from a device-code-authorized session · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Entra ID device-code grant to first-time user via Microsoft Authentication Broker AIExploitation High
Hunts the first-ever successful sign-in to the Microsoft Authentication Broker app (AppId 29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e) for a given user. This is the exact first-party client Storm-2372 and EvilTokens-style kits drive victims into via the OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant to mint a token / PRT, so a user appearing on it for the first time is a high-fidelity device-code-phishing signal. Rationale: Anchors on the concrete first-party AppId 29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e (Microsoft Authentication Broker) that Storm-2372's device-code campaign used to register a device / harvest a PRT; a first-time appearance per user is a strong, low-noise device-code-phishing indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/
ATT&CKT1528 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.All_Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately running `az login`/`Connect-AzAccount` device-code flow for the first time
  • New hire onboarding onto Intune/Windows Hello registering a device via the broker
  • IT rolling out a CLI or VS Code tunnel workflow to a new team
  • User re-registering a wiped/replaced laptop
  • Automated first-run of a build agent using the broker
Suppression filter
| where not (ClientAppUsed == "Mobile Apps and Desktop clients" and DeviceTrustType in ("Azure AD joined","Hybrid Azure AD joined") and Country in ("US"))  // compliant/managed device onboarding from expected geo
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the sign-in's IP/ASN, UserAgent and geo; check whether the same user had an interactive sign-in from a different IP minutes earlier (victim entered code, attacker redeemed). Confirm no legit CLI/Intune onboarding is scheduled for this user. 2) Contain: if unexplained, revoke the user's refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession / 'Revoke sessions'), disable the account, and remove any device registered in the last hour. 3) Hunt: pivot on the token — check AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs for the same session touching multiple resources, and OfficeActivity for mailbox/SharePoint bulk access.
let AuthBroker = "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e";  // Microsoft Authentication Broker (Storm-2372 device-code / PRT registration app)
let Baseline = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where ErrorCode == 0 and ApplicationId == AuthBroker
    | summarize by AccountUpn;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ErrorCode == 0 and ApplicationId == AuthBroker
| where AccountUpn !endswith "$"
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on AccountUpn
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, Country, City, UserAgent, ClientAppUsed, DeviceTrustType
| order by Timestamp desc
let AuthBroker = "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e";  // Microsoft Authentication Broker (Storm-2372 device-code / PRT app)
let Baseline = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where ResultType == 0 and AppId == AuthBroker
    | summarize by UserPrincipalName;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == 0 and AppId == AuthBroker
| where UserPrincipalName !endswith "$"
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on UserPrincipalName
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, Location, UserAgent, ClientAppUsed, AuthenticationDetails
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Device-code sign-in from country never seen for the user (stolen-code redemption) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts successful sign-ins to device-code-capable first-party client apps (Authentication Broker, Azure CLI/PowerShell, Office, VS Code) from a country the user has never signed in from in the prior 30 days. Device code phishing separates code entry (victim) from token redemption (attacker), so the redeeming client frequently lands in a new geography. Rationale: Uses the real device-code-capable first-party AppIds plus a 30-day per-user country baseline (leftanti) to surface the geographic split between victim code-entry and attacker token-redemption that defines device-code phishing. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078/004/
ATT&CKT1528 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.All_Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Traveling employee legitimately using Azure CLI abroad for the first time
  • Corporate VPN / cloud egress that geo-locates to a datacenter country
  • Contractor onboarding from a new region
  • Roaming mobile user near a border where geo-IP flips country
  • M365 client re-authenticating through a proxy in another country
Suppression filter
| where not (IsAnonymousProxy == false and AppId == "04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46" and Country in ("GB","US","IE","DE"))  // scope to unexpected geos; tune allowed travel countries per org
Response runbook
1) Triage: compare the new-country sign-in IP/ASN against the user's interactive sign-in in the prior 30 min; anonymizer/hosting ASN or a country the user cannot plausibly be in raises confidence. 2) Contain: revoke sessions, force password reset, and apply a CA block on device-code flow for the user if unexplained. 3) Hunt: check AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs for the same token fanning out to Mail/SharePoint and AuditLogs for a new device registration.
let DeviceCodeApps = dynamic(["29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e","04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46","1950a258-227b-4e31-a9cf-717495945fc2","d3590ed6-52b3-4102-aeff-aad2292ab01c","aebc6443-996d-45c2-90f0-388ff96faa56"]);  // device-code-capable first-party clients
let Baseline = AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where ErrorCode == 0 and isnotempty(Country)
    | summarize by AccountUpn, Country;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where ApplicationId in (DeviceCodeApps)
| where isnotempty(Country) and AccountUpn !endswith "$"
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on AccountUpn, Country
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, AppDisplayName, ApplicationId, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, Country, City, UserAgent, IsAnonymousProxy
| order by Timestamp desc
let DeviceCodeApps = dynamic(["29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e","04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46","1950a258-227b-4e31-a9cf-717495945fc2","d3590ed6-52b3-4102-aeff-aad2292ab01c","aebc6443-996d-45c2-90f0-388ff96faa56"]);
let Baseline = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where ResultType == 0 and isnotempty(Location)
    | summarize by UserPrincipalName, Location;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where AppId in (DeviceCodeApps)
| where isnotempty(Location) and UserPrincipalName !endswith "$"
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on UserPrincipalName, Location
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, AppId, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, Location, UserAgent, AuthenticationDetails
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Stolen device-code token fanning out to multiple SSO resources within the hour AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts a single device-code-authorized session whose non-interactive token reaches an unusually high number of distinct Entra resources within one hour. This models the article's 'stolen token to full SSO-level access' escalation, where one grant is replayed across mailbox, SharePoint, Graph and other SSO apps. Rationale: Threshold + 1h temporal aggregation over non-interactive sign-ins from the concrete device-code AppIds captures the article's token-to-SSO privilege-escalation fan-out without needing endpoint telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/001/
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.All_Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin running broad Graph/Azure CLI automation touching many services
  • CI/CD or IaC pipeline authenticating via Azure PowerShell across resources
  • Power user opening Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and OneDrive in quick succession
  • Security tooling enumerating tenant resources with a service account
  • Migration/backup job walking many SharePoint sites
Suppression filter
| where not (array_length(IPs) == 1 and UserPrincipalName has_any ("svc-","automation","pipeline"))  // single-source service/automation identities
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the IPs set — a single source IP is normal automation; a mismatch between the sign-in IP and the user's usual geo, or an anonymizer ASN, raises confidence. Cross-check for a preceding first-time Authentication Broker sign-in. 2) Contain: revoke refresh tokens, disable the account, and quarantine any device registered in the window. 3) Hunt: pull OfficeActivity for MailItemsAccessed/FileDownloaded bursts and AuditLogs for inbox-rule creation (BEC) tied to the same UPN.
let DeviceCodeApps = dynamic(["29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e","04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46","1950a258-227b-4e31-a9cf-717495945fc2","d3590ed6-52b3-4102-aeff-aad2292ab01c","aebc6443-996d-45c2-90f0-388ff96faa56"]);
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ErrorCode == 0 and IsInteractive == false
| where ApplicationId in (DeviceCodeApps)
| where AccountUpn !endswith "$"
| summarize DistinctResources = dcount(ResourceDisplayName), Resources = make_set(ResourceDisplayName, 25), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), StartTime = min(Timestamp), EndTime = max(Timestamp) by AccountUpn, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where DistinctResources >= 5   // 1 device-code token hitting >=5 distinct SSO resources in 1h (legit CLI/PS use ~1-3)
| order by DistinctResources desc
let DeviceCodeApps = dynamic(["29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e","04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46","1950a258-227b-4e31-a9cf-717495945fc2","d3590ed6-52b3-4102-aeff-aad2292ab01c","aebc6443-996d-45c2-90f0-388ff96faa56"]);
AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where AppId in (DeviceCodeApps)
| where UserPrincipalName !endswith "$"
| summarize DistinctResources = dcount(ResourceDisplayName), Resources = make_set(ResourceDisplayName, 25), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), StartTime = min(TimeGenerated), EndTime = max(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DistinctResources >= 5   // 1 device-code token hitting >=5 distinct SSO resources in 1h (P99 legit ~2-3)
| order by DistinctResources desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.status.errorCode:0 @properties.appDisplayName:("Microsoft Authentication Broker" OR "Microsoft Azure CLI" OR "Microsoft Azure PowerShell" OR "Microsoft Office")
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` dc(Authentication.dest) as distinctResources values(Authentication.dest) as resources values(Authentication.src) as srcIPs min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success Authentication.app IN ("Microsoft Authentication Broker","Microsoft Azure CLI","Microsoft Azure PowerShell","Microsoft Office","Visual Studio Code") by Authentication.user _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where distinctResources>=5
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(Authentication.dest) as distinctResources values(Authentication.dest) as resources values(Authentication.src) as srcIPs min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success Authentication.app IN ("Microsoft Authentication Broker","Microsoft Azure CLI","Microsoft Azure PowerShell","Microsoft Office","Visual Studio Code") by Authentication.user _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where distinctResources>=5
New Entra device registration shortly after a device-code grant (PRT persistence) AIInstallation Medium
Correlates a successful Microsoft Authentication Broker sign-in with an Entra device-registration audit event by the same user within one hour. This is the ARToken/Storm-2372 PRT-persistence step, where a phished device-code token is used to join a rogue device and obtain a self-renewing Primary Refresh Token. Rationale: Ties the concrete Authentication Broker AppId sign-in to the Entra 'Register device' / 'Add registered owner to device' audit operations within 1h — the exact PRT-persistence chain the article attributes to ARToken and Storm-2372. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/005/
ATT&CKT1098.005 T1550.001
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Intune/Autopilot device enrollment
  • User adding a new personal device via BYOD registration
  • IT bulk-registering replacement laptops
  • Windows Hello for Business provisioning on a new machine
  • Hybrid join sync registering an on-prem device
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatorIP == SignInIP and SignInLocation in ("GB","US"))  // registration from the same expected corporate egress as the sign-in
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify the registered device's OS/name against the user's known assets and compare the registration IP to the user's normal geo; an unmanaged/unexpected device from a foreign IP is high-confidence. 2) Contain: disable/delete the newly registered device object, revoke the user's PRT and refresh tokens, and reset credentials. 3) Hunt: search AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs for tokens issued to the rogue device and AuditLogs for subsequent role/consent grants.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where ApplicationId == "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e"   // Microsoft Authentication Broker
| where ResourceDisplayName has "Device Registration"
| where AccountUpn !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, IPAddress, Country, City, UserAgent, DeviceName, AadDeviceId, DeviceTrustType
| order by Timestamp desc
let AuthBroker = "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e";  // Microsoft Authentication Broker
let RecentDeviceCode = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ResultType == 0 and AppId == AuthBroker
    | project SignInTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, SignInIP = IPAddress, SignInLocation = Location;
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where OperationName in ("Add registered owner to device","Register device","Add device")
| where Result == "success"
| extend InitiatorUPN = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), InitiatorIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress), TargetDevice = tostring(TargetResources[0].displayName)
| join kind=inner RecentDeviceCode on $left.InitiatorUPN == $right.UserPrincipalName
| where TimeGenerated between (SignInTime .. SignInTime + 1h)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, InitiatorUPN, InitiatorIP, SignInTime, SignInIP, SignInLocation, TargetDevice
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:("Register device" OR "Add registered owner to device" OR "Add device")
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Change where Change.action=created Change.object_category="device" (Change.command="Add device" OR Change.command="Register device" OR Change.command="Add registered owner to device") by Change.user Change.src _time | `drop_dm_object_name(Change)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Change where Change.action=created Change.object_category="device" (Change.command="Add device" OR Change.command="Register device" OR Change.command="Add registered owner to device") by Change.user Change.src _time | `drop_dm_object_name(Change)`
Phishing email delivering a Microsoft/GitHub device-login URL AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound delivered email containing links to legitimate device-authorization portals (microsoft.com/devicelogin, oauth2/deviceauth, github.com/login/device, AWS verification). Because the victim enters the code on a real provider URL, the lure email carrying that portal link is one of the few network-observable initial-access artifacts of device-code phishing. Rationale: Matches on the literal device-authorization portal path tokens (devicelogin, oauth2/deviceauth, login/device) the article names as the pages victims are steered to — legitimate provider URLs that email gateways won't block, making delivered-inbox delivery a high-fidelity lure signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/002/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1528
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Microsoft/GitHub onboarding email instructing CLI device login
  • Internal IT help-desk mail linking to aka.ms/devicelogin for setup
  • SaaS vendor genuinely using device-code enrollment
  • Security-awareness training simulation using the same URL
  • Newsletter/blog quoting the device-login URL as text
Suppression filter
| where not (SenderMailFromDomain in~ ("microsoft.com","azure.com","github.com") and PhishConfidenceLevel != "High")  // genuine first-party onboarding mail
Response runbook
1) Triage: review sender domain/SPF-DKIM-DMARC and whether the message was expected; a look-alike or unauthenticated external sender with the device-login link is high-confidence phish. 2) Contain: soft-delete/quarantine the message org-wide via Explorer, block the sender, and warn recipients not to enter any code. 3) Hunt: for any recipient, check SigninLogs for a Microsoft Authentication Broker / device-code app grant within an hour of delivery and revoke if found.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
| join kind=inner (
    EmailUrlInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where Url has_any ("devicelogin","oauth2/deviceauth","login/device","aka.ms/devicelogin","amazon.com/verification")
    | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, Url, UrlDomain, DeliveryLocation, PhishConfidenceLevel
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound" and DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
| join kind=inner (
    EmailUrlInfo
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where Url has_any ("devicelogin","oauth2/deviceauth","login/device","aka.ms/devicelogin","amazon.com/verification")
    | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project TimeGenerated, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, Url, UrlDomain, DeliveryLocation, PhishConfidenceLevel
| order by TimeGenerated desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Email where Email.direction=inbound (Email.url="*devicelogin*" OR Email.url="*oauth2/deviceauth*" OR Email.url="*login/device*" OR Email.url="*aka.ms/devicelogin*") by Email.src_user Email.recipient Email.subject Email.url _time | `drop_dm_object_name(Email)` | sort - _time
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Email where Email.direction=inbound (Email.url="*devicelogin*" OR Email.url="*oauth2/deviceauth*" OR Email.url="*login/device*" OR Email.url="*aka.ms/devicelogin*") by Email.src_user Email.recipient Email.subject Email.url _time | `drop_dm_object_name(Email)` | sort - _time
Bulk mailbox and SharePoint collection from a device-code-authorized session AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates a device-code app sign-in with a burst of mailbox-read, file-download and search operations by the same user within 6 hours. This targets the ARToken feature set the article calls out (mailbox access + SharePoint exfiltration), catching the collection stage that follows a stolen device-code token. Rationale: Joins device-code app sign-ins to a same-user burst of MailItemsAccessed / FileDownloaded / SearchQueryPerformed within 6h, directly modeling the article's ARToken 'mailbox access + SharePoint exfiltration' collection features rather than a generic mail-volume alert. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1114/002/
ATT&CKT1114.002 T1213.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • eDiscovery / compliance search legitimately reading many mailbox items
  • User doing a large legitimate OneDrive/SharePoint sync after onboarding
  • Backup or migration tooling downloading many files
  • Executive assistant with delegated access reading multiple mailboxes
  • Bulk report export by a data analyst
Suppression filter
| where not (NormUser has_any ("ediscovery","compliance","svc-backup") or ClientIP in (""))  // exclude known compliance/backup service identities (populate ClientIP allowlist per tenant)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the ClientIP/token maps to a device-code app sign-in (not a normal browser session) and check whether the volume aligns with the user's role. 2) Contain: revoke sessions, disable the account, and place a hold on the mailbox/sites touched to preserve evidence. 3) Hunt: look for inbox-rule creation, forwarding, or SharePoint sharing changes by the same UPN, and any newly registered device from the earlier device-code grant.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType in ("MailItemsAccessed","FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull","SearchQueryPerformed")
| summarize Ops = count(), MailAccessed = countif(ActionType == "MailItemsAccessed"), Downloads = countif(ActionType in ("FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull")), Searches = countif(ActionType == "SearchQueryPerformed") by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where Ops >= 50   // bulk mailbox/SharePoint burst; correlate account with a recent device-code sign-in (AADSignInEventsBeta AppId 29d9ed98-...)
| order by Ops desc
let DeviceCodeApps = dynamic(["29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e","04b07795-8ddb-461a-bbee-02f9e1bf7b46","1950a258-227b-4e31-a9cf-717495945fc2","d3590ed6-52b3-4102-aeff-aad2292ab01c"]);
let DeviceCodeUsers = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ResultType == 0 and AppId in (DeviceCodeApps)
    | summarize DeviceCodeSignIn = min(TimeGenerated) by NormUser = tolower(UserPrincipalName);
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where Operation in ("MailItemsAccessed","FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull","SearchQueryPerformed","FileAccessed")
| extend NormUser = tolower(UserId)
| join kind=inner DeviceCodeUsers on NormUser
| where TimeGenerated between (DeviceCodeSignIn .. DeviceCodeSignIn + 6h)
| summarize Ops = count(), MailAccessed = countif(Operation == "MailItemsAccessed"), Downloads = countif(Operation in ("FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull")), Searches = countif(Operation == "SearchQueryPerformed") by NormUser, ClientIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where Ops >= 50   // bulk collection burst within 6h of a device-code sign-in (P99 interactive user < 30/hr)
| order by Ops desc
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count as ops sum(eval(if(Operation=="MailItemsAccessed",1,0))) as mailAccessed sum(eval(if(Operation IN ("FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull"),1,0))) as downloads from datamodel=Email where Email.Operation IN ("MailItemsAccessed","FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull","SearchQueryPerformed") by Email.user Email.src _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Email)` | where ops>=50
| tstats summariesonly=false count as ops sum(eval(if(Operation=="MailItemsAccessed",1,0))) as mailAccessed sum(eval(if(Operation IN ("FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull"),1,0))) as downloads from datamodel=Email where Email.Operation IN ("MailItemsAccessed","FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull","SearchQueryPerformed") by Email.user Email.src _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Email)` | where ops>=50
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

ImFileEvent

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

Chinese Hacker Commands DeepSeek via Telegram to Launch Autonomous Attacks

The Hacker News
2026-07-31 14 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 says a Chinese-speaking threat actor used DeepSeek through the open-source Hermes Agent framework to launch attacks autonomously. After an initial Telegram instruction, the agent found internet-facing systems and selected public exploits. The researchers recovered no further operator input in the session. The operator, tracked through the aliases knaithe and KnYuan,

Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Chinese Hacker Commands DeepSeek via Telegram to Launch Autonomous Attacks
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Hermes AI agent OPSEC leak: python3 -m http.server 8888 from home directory · [LLM] Autonomous attack-agent egress to LLM inference APIs from non-browser process · [LLM] Hermes agent C2 fingerprint: Telegram Bot API + LLM inference API from same host · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Marimo pre-auth RCE (CVE-2026-39987): marimo/python parent spawning a shell (PTY) AIExploitation High
Hunts the confirmed-successful track of this campaign: the DeepSeek/Hermes agent exploited CVE-2026-39987 on 11 Marimo notebook servers via the unauthenticated /terminal/ws WebSocket, which drops a full PTY. Detects the Marimo notebook process (python) spawning an interactive shell child — the on-host footprint of that terminal takeover. Rationale: Anchors on the confirmed track (Unit 42: command execution on 11 Marimo instances via CVE-2026-39987) and the specific exploit primitive — the unauthenticated /terminal/ws endpoint yields a PTY, so the notebook's python process becomes the parent of an interactive shell. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/ • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/marimo-oss-python-notebook-rce-from-disclosure-to-exploitation-in-under-10-hours • https://securityaffairs.com/190623/hacking/cve-2026-39987-marimo-rce-exploited-in-hours-after-disclosure.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A data scientist legitimately opening the Marimo built-in terminal to run shell commands in a notebook
  • Marimo notebook cells that call subprocess/os.system as part of normal analytics pipelines
  • CI/CD or container entrypoints where marimo is launched then a shell wrapper runs
  • Jupyter-style kernels co-located with marimo triggering shell utilities (git, pip)
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl","wget","/tmp/","nc ","bash -i","python -c","base64") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "/terminal/ws"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child shell's ProcessCommandLine and subsequent process tree on the host; confirm whether the marimo instance is internet-facing and its version (<0.23.0 is vulnerable). Check web/reverse-proxy logs for GET/Upgrade to /terminal/ws from external IPs. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the marimo service, block inbound to the notebook port, and rotate any credentials/API keys readable from that host (campaign completed credential theft in <3 min). 3) Hunt: search the same host for outbound to api.telegram.org / api.deepseek.com / code.newcli.com and for python3 -m http.server 8888, which indicate the Hermes agent staged there.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "marimo" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "marimo")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ash")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildProcess = FileName, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where (ParentProcessCommandLine has "marimo" or ParentProcessName has "marimo")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ash")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow CVE-2026-33017 exploitation: scanner tooling and langflow exec-to-shell AIExploitation Medium
Detects both sides of the Langflow track: the attacker's mass-scanner command line (langflow_poc.py --scan-file langflow_targets.txt --threads 10) recovered from the exposed Hermes home directory, and victim-side exploitation where the Langflow python process (exec() code injection) spawns a shell. Rationale: Uses two article-specific strings: the exact scanner invocation (langflow_poc.py --scan-file langflow_targets.txt --threads 10) recovered from /home/worker, and the CVE-2026-33017 exec() primitive that makes the Langflow python worker the parent of a shell. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/ • https://www.sonicwall.com/blog/langflow-ai-code-injection-to-rce-flaw • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/cisa-flags-langflow-rce-tomcat-and-n.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006 T1595.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team running the public Langflow PoC internally for patch validation
  • Langflow custom components that legitimately shell out (git, pip install of a component)
  • A developer named a local file langflow_targets.txt for unrelated reasons
  • Langflow container entrypoint scripts invoking bash during startup
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pytest","patch-validation") or AccountName in~ ("appsvc","ci-runner"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: if the scanner strings hit, treat the host as an attacker/staging box — enumerate its outbound targets and shell history. If the exploit branch hit, confirm the Langflow version (<1.9.0 vulnerable) and inspect the child shell command line. 2) Contain: isolate the host, take the Langflow service offline, and block the notebook/UI port from the internet. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for python3 -m http.server 8888, api.deepseek.com egress, and Telegram C2; review Langflow app logs for POSTs with embedded Python in node definitions.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("langflow_poc.py","langflow_targets.txt")
    or (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "langflow" and FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ash"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildProcess = FileName, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("langflow_poc.py","langflow_targets.txt")
    or (ParentProcessCommandLine has "langflow" and ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ash"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

n8n exploit chain (CVE-2026-21858 + CVE-2025-68613): node process spawning a shell AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the n8n track where the agent combined the unauthenticated file-access flaw CVE-2026-21858 with the expression-injection flaw CVE-2025-68613. Detects the n8n Node.js process spawning an OS command interpreter — the execution footprint of the chained expression-injection RCE. Rationale: Ties to the specific two-CVE n8n chain named by Unit 42; the expression-injection flaw yields OS command execution, so a legitimate n8n Node worker becoming the parent of a shell is the on-host signature even though this campaign's n8n attempts failed on config. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hacker-uses-deepseek-ai-to-autonomously-attack-vulnerable-servers/

  • n8n community nodes that shell out to CLI tools (ffmpeg, git, imagemagick)
  • n8n container healthchecks or entrypoint wrappers invoking sh
  • Backup/cron jobs running under the n8n service account
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ffmpeg","imagemagick","/usr/bin/git") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "Execute Command")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child shell command line and the parent n8n workflow/expression that triggered it; verify n8n version (patched at 1.121.1 for both flaws). 2) Contain: isolate the host, disable public access to the n8n editor/webhook endpoints, and audit which workflows have Execute Command nodes. 3) Hunt: check the same host for outbound LLM/Telegram C2 and http.server 8888; review n8n audit logs for unauthenticated file-access requests (CVE-2026-21858).

Hermes AI agent OPSEC leak: python3 -m http.server 8888 from home directory AICommand & Control High
Detects the exact misstep that exposed this operation: the Hermes Agent started 'python3 -m http.server 8888' from /home/worker, inadvertently serving its API keys, exploit scripts, target lists and session logs. Flags this specific ad-hoc web server, especially under the 'worker' account, as an indicator of a staged AI attack-agent host. Rationale: Uses the literal command line 'python3 -m http.server 8888' and the 'worker' account (from /home/worker) that Unit 42 reported as the operation-exposing artifact — an extremely specific, low-noise indicator of a Hermes/DeepSeek agent staging host. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/08/03/deepseek-ai-autonomous-cyberattacks-hermes-agent/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1608.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer quickly serving files locally with python -m http.server 8888 for testing
  • Container demos or documentation servers bound to 8888
  • Data scientists sharing a directory over http.server on an internal box
  • Jupyter/other tooling that a user chose to expose on port 8888
Suppression filter
| where not (AccountName in~ ("jenkins","gitlab-runner") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pytest","mkdocs","jupyter"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: on hit, immediately capture the serving directory contents and shell history (~/.bash_history) — the campaign exposed API keys, exploit scripts, target lists and AI session logs this way. Confirm whether the port is reachable externally. 2) Contain: kill the http.server process, isolate the host, and rotate every credential/API key found in the served directory. 3) Hunt: enumerate the host's outbound connections to api.deepseek.com, dashscope.aliyuncs.com, code.newcli.com and api.telegram.org, and look for langflow_poc.py / target list files to scope the agent's activity.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("python3","python")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "http.server" and ProcessCommandLine has "8888"
| extend HighFidelity = iff(AccountName =~ "worker", "worker-account", "other")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, HighFidelity, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python3","python")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "http.server" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "8888"
| extend HighFidelity = iff(ActorUsername =~ "worker", "worker-account", "other")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, HighFidelity, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Autonomous attack-agent egress to LLM inference APIs from non-browser process AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the reasoning-engine traffic of the Hermes agent: outbound HTTPS to api.deepseek.com, dashscope.aliyuncs.com (Qwen) or the code.newcli.com proxy (Claude Code/Codex routing) initiated by a headless/server process (python, node, curl) rather than a browser. That combination indicates unsanctioned autonomous LLM tooling driving attacks, not human chat use. Rationale: Uses the exact LLM/proxy endpoints Unit 42 recovered (api.deepseek.com, dashscope.aliyuncs.com, code.newcli.com); scoping to non-browser initiating processes distinguishes autonomous agent tooling from sanctioned human AI use. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/08/03/deepseek-ai-autonomous-cyberattacks-hermes-agent/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sanctioned internal AI service/agent legitimately calling DeepSeek or Qwen APIs from a backend
  • Developers testing LLM SDKs with curl/python from a workstation
  • CI jobs that call code assistants via API
  • Data-pipeline scripts summarizing content via DeepSeek/Qwen
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("ai-gateway01","sanctioned-llm-proxy") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "approved-agent"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and its command line; determine if the host is a sanctioned AI workload or an internet-facing app server (the latter is highly suspicious). Check for co-occurring exploit tooling on the host. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, isolate the host, block the LLM/proxy domains at egress for that segment, and preserve the process's working directory. 3) Hunt: correlate with api.telegram.org egress and http.server 8888 on the same host, and review whether the host also targeted Langflow/n8n/Marimo/NetScaler.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.deepseek.com","dashscope.aliyuncs.com","code.newcli.com")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python3","python","node","curl","wget","go","sh","bash")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize Count = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Procs = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 8), Domains = make_set(RemoteUrl, 8) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("api.deepseek.com","dashscope.aliyuncs.com","code.newcli.com")
| summarize Count = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Domains = make_set(DnsQuery, 8) by SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname
| order by FirstSeen desc

Hermes agent C2 fingerprint: Telegram Bot API + LLM inference API from same host AICommand & Control High
High-fidelity correlation for this campaign's control channel: the operator commanded the agent over Telegram, while DeepSeek/Qwen served as the reasoning engine. Alerts when a single host contacts api.telegram.org and an LLM inference endpoint (api.deepseek.com / dashscope.aliyuncs.com / code.newcli.com) within a short window — the dual-destination signature of a Telegram-driven autonomous attack agent. Rationale: Combines the two named control components — Telegram command channel (api.telegram.org) and the LLM reasoning APIs — into a single per-host correlation; requiring both destinations within an hour makes this far higher fidelity than either domain alone. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hacker-uses-deepseek-ai-to-autonomously-attack-vulnerable-servers/
ATT&CKT1102.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user on a workstation who both uses a Telegram desktop client and a DeepSeek/Qwen chat app
  • A monitoring bot that posts to Telegram while a separate app on the same host uses an LLM API
  • Developer laptops with Telegram plus AI coding assistants
  • NAT/proxy egress collapsing many users to one source IP (Sentinel SrcIpAddr variant)
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName has_any ("srv","app","web","api") or DeviceName !has "laptop"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host type — a server or internet-facing app host contacting both Telegram and an LLM API is high-suspicion; identify the initiating processes. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block api.telegram.org and the LLM/proxy domains for that segment, and capture memory/working directory before shutdown. 3) Hunt: search the host for http.server 8888, langflow_poc.py, target-list files and exploit scripts, and review which external targets it scanned or exploited (Langflow/n8n/Marimo/NetScaler).
let win = 1h;
let llm = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.deepseek.com","dashscope.aliyuncs.com","code.newcli.com")
    | project DeviceId, DeviceName, LlmTime = Timestamp, LlmUrl = RemoteUrl, LlmProc = InitiatingProcessFileName;
DeviceNetworkEvents

| join kind=inner llm on DeviceId
| where abs(datetime_diff('minute', TgTime, LlmTime)) <= 60

| order by TgTime desc
let win = 1h;

    | where DnsQuery has_any ("api.deepseek.com","dashscope.aliyuncs.com","code.newcli.com")
    | project SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, LlmTime = TimeGenerated, LlmQuery = DnsQuery;
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DnsQuery has "api.telegram.org"
| project SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, TgTime = TimeGenerated
| join kind=inner llm on SrcIpAddr
| where abs(datetime_diff('minute', TgTime, LlmTime)) <= 60
| project SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, TgTime, LlmTime, LlmQuery
| order by TgTime desc

NetScaler CVE-2026-3055 SAML IdP exposure and session-cookie (NSC_AAAC) abuse AIExploitation Medium
Covers the confirmed data-exfiltration track: the operator used the NetScaler memory-overread flaw CVE-2026-3055 against ADC/Gateway appliances configured as SAML identity providers. Surfaces vulnerable/exposed NetScaler assets and flags NSC_AAAC AAA-session-cookie activity against the SAML IdP endpoints indicative of the overread/session hijack. Rationale: Anchors on the confirmed-successful NetScaler track: the CVE-2026-3055 SAML-IdP condition (add authentication samlIdPProfile) plus the NSC_AAAC AAA-session cookie Unit 42 cited as the session-hijack indicator, combined with a TVM exposure check for the exact CVE. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hacker-uses-deepseek-ai-to-autonomously-attack-vulnerable-servers/
ATT&CKT1190 T1539 T1005
Data sourcesVulnerabilities Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate high-volume SAML SSO logins during business hours from a corporate egress IP
  • Load balancers or health monitors probing the SAML endpoint
  • Federated partners generating bursts of SAML AuthnRequests
  • Vulnerability scanners the org itself runs against the NetScaler
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<corporate_egress_ips_via_watchlist>") | where isnotempty(SourceIP)
Response runbook
1) Triage: for TVM hits, confirm the appliance is customer-managed, internet-facing, and configured as a SAML IdP (add authentication samlIdPProfile). For log hits, review the source IPs hitting the SAML endpoint and whether NSC_AAAC sessions are reused from new geolocations. 2) Contain: install the fixed NetScaler build per Citrix bulletin, invalidate all AAA sessions, and rotate SAML signing material. 3) Hunt: correlate suspect source IPs with the campaign's other activity, and review downstream apps for logins using hijacked NetScaler sessions.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-3055"
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | where IsInternetFacing == true | summarize by DeviceId, IsInternetFacing) on DeviceId

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

     | rename dest AS src]

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Network Anomaly Detection in KATA

Securelist (Kaspersky)
2026-07-31 8 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

An analysis of how Network Anomaly Detection (NAD) rules work within Kaspersky Anti Targeted Attack, using Kerberoasting and DNS tunneling attacks as examples.

ATT&CKT1021.001 T1190 T1558 T1558.003
Domainstestinglab.ru crust.testinglab.ru
